rows.etymology: 1196. Kal. buṣ ‘mature, uncastrated, virile, able to reproduce (only billy-goats, rams and bulls)’ < OIA vr̥ṣa- or vŕ̥ṣan- ‘male; bull, etc’. Note: Here etymologically not related is Kal. brúc̣ak ‘testicles’ (even though it could be a case of spontaneous affrication as in Klm. mäĩṣ ∼ mäĩc̣ ‘buffalo’ < OIA mahiṣá- ‘buffalo’ [9964]), but has probably cognates discussed below p. 793 sub kuškuḷúk ‘testicles’.

rows.etymology: 117. Kal. phḷis ‘stark naked’ as in se phḷis thi gháay ásta ‘he was naked near the ravine’, Kho. phḷís ‘naked’ and phḷís nisík ‘to be completely naked’ < PIE *bhosós ‘bare, naked’. There are several possibilities to explain the -ḷ-: (a) it is an emphatic particle perhaps also found in Kal. kḷok hik ‘to stop laying eggs’ (with cognate but semantically inverted Kho. kḷok ‘state of a hen after laying a clutch of eggs, when she is ready to hatch them, broody’) is somehow related with Kal. kakavaṅk ‘chicken’, koḷučúyak ‘chick, hatchling’ and Bur. kaák ét-, kaák-kaák ét- ‘to cluck (hen while laying eggs)’ and Pr. muṣ-kakag ‘rooster’, kakag ‘chicken’ and vəst'ī-kakag ‘hen’ which cf. with onomatopoeic PIE *gag- ‘cackle’ (but note also onomatopoeic H. kuk-kuk and Bur. kukúk ét- ‘the clucking of a hen’) (RECHECK, see also Nyah Kur khlɔ̀ɔk ‘litter, brood (of chicks. . . ’) and Proto-Pramic *klih to hatch)’; (b) it is an element ‘very’ for which cf. Kho. leˑi ‘very’ which has been borrowed into Kal. (Morgenstierne [1973a: 204]); (c) according to Pokorny, PIE *bʰosós may be connected with PIE *bʰes- ‘rub’ where, as he points out, one finds (IEW: 146) Gr. ψιλóς ‘bleak, bare, uncovered; kahl, bloß’.

rows.gloss: if an egg falls it will become smashed
rows.etymology: 174. Kal. lep ‘flat, smashed’ as in óṇḍrak pe átav hav, lep híu ‘if an egg falls it will become smashed’ and lep nástan ‘flat-nosed, squashed-nosed’ — S. lap ‘the full of one hand open’ < PIE *lēp-, lōp-, ləp- ‘flat; palm’ etc. (IEW: 679) resp. *leh2p-eh2- (Kroonen [2013: 340f.]), reflected also e.g. in Old High German lappo ‘flat hand’ and Swedish labb ‘paw’. Under this lemma, Pokorny lists also Lith. lãpas ‘leaf’ (and there is Latv. lapa ‘leaf’), but this is probably wrong and they are rather connected with OL ‘leaf’ words mentioned above p. 63. The lemma was borrowed into FU (see Joki 1973: 277) where Joki quotes Fi. lapa ‘prow, scapula; Bug, Schulterblatt’ etc.

origin_lemma.gloss: lump, clod, piece; mouthful, ball of rice &c.; calf of leg
origin_lemma.etymology: 8168 píṇḍa m. 'lump, clod, piece' RV., 'mouthful, ball of rice &c.' Gr̥Śr., 'calf of leg' Mālatīm., piṇḍaka- m.n. 'lump' Suśr., °ḍī- f. 'lump, lump of food' Āpast., °ḍikā- f. 'any fleshy swelling, esp. calf of leg' Yājñ. (cf. piṇḍilá- 'having large calves' lex. and → Psht. paṇḍaī 'calf of leg' EVP 57). [For 'lump' see also piḍaka-, *pēṇḍa-, *pēṇḍha-, *pēḍa-, *pēḍha-, *pēnda-, *pēntha, *puṇḍa-, *pōdda-, *pōnda-. This variety of phonetic form suggests non-Aryan (← Mu. PMWS 142, 162; ← Drav. T. Burrow TPS 1946, 23) rather than IE. origin EWA ii 275. P. Thieme's derivation < *piṁṣṭa- (ZDMG 93, 133) is phonetically unacceptable]
origin_lemma.tags: m RV Gr̥Śr Mālatīm Early-Vedic Classical

rows.etymology: 653. Bng. tɔpɔ n.m. ‘place or goal within reach or according to one’s capacity; reach, range’, tɔpɛ kɛ adv. ‘in a right or fixed place’, cf. OIA (Daś.) tatpada ‘the place of that’ — here perhaps also Bur.ys. thop ‘target (in the sense of Zielscheibe)’ and Wg. tapˈa ‘group, party, factionist (in playing)’ because of padá- also meaning ‘standpoint, position, rank’.

rows.etymology: 6. Bur. mukhóoro ‘flatterer, sycophant, sweet talker’, Sh. mukhóoro ‘speaker of a group’, Kal. mukhár ‘face to face’ — Sant. mukhɔrɔ ‘eloquent, rhetorical, ready speaker’. Berger suggests connection with OIA múkhya- ‘pertaining to face or mouth’ (10174) but the words rather appear to be (apart from Sh. and Kal.) early borrowings of mukhará- ‘talkative’ (10167). However, the OIA lemma múkha- ‘mouth, face’ (10158) appears quite confusing and I need to point out here that its ultimate origin is unclear (see EWA). There appear to exist allomorphs with unaspirated velar consonant: probably Kal. (-)muki ‘dispositioned’ as in košan-múki ‘happy-dispositioned’, zaŋgar- múki ‘sour-dispositioned’ and mukhár múki hik ‘to be humiliated’ — Ju. muko and So. mukka both ‘face’ — Kensiu muka ‘face’, Semelai mukaʔ ‘face, front’, Temiar mukaʔ ‘face’, Khmer muk ‘face’, Surin Khmer muʔ ‘in front of; a face; a sharp edge’, Mon mə̀k ‘face’, Riang mɔk² ‘face’, Pear and Chong muk ‘visage’ — Austronesian Malay muka ‘face’. It is difficult to assume that all modern forms are ultimately borrowings from OIA. After all, Sanskrit borrowings into the Mon-Khmer Aslian branch are extremely rare (yet, they may have come there via Malay lingua franca).

rows.etymology: 1141. Sh.koh. bās ‘evening’, Sh.gur. bās ‘in the evening’ (Wilson [1899b: 100]), Sh.dras. bas ‘eveninng’ and Sh. “bás” ‘at night’ (Leitner [1889: 17]), Sh.gult. baás ‘yester- day’ (data received from Ruth Schmidt) which contrasts with regard to accent with báas ‘overnight stay’ (< OIA vāsá- ‘abode; staying’), and here probably also Kal. ósi ‘last night’, osíakas ‘evening time from seven to ten o’clock’ (with unclear second component), doṣ ósi ‘the night before last’ as in doṣ ósi tu ne íta ái ‘you didn’t come the night before last’ (appears to be a quasi synonym compound with first compo- nent < OIA doṣá̄- ‘night, night personified’ [6590]), and probably even osióna ‘the last amount of grain before one’s supply is finished’ (with second component < OIA ánna- ‘corn in general’ [395] found e.g. in Sh. ȏn ‘grain [in general]’), and Pr. asra ‘that to the left(?), to the west’ (Morgenstierne [1949: 225, 250]) (əsˈəra ‘lateral, sideways; seitlich’ [Buddruss und Degener]). Phonologically unlikely is relationship of all these forms with OIA avás and avástāt ‘downwards’, but a plausible possibility seems to be derivation < OIA (ŚāṅkhŚr) avasavi ‘to the left’ where second component is cognate with OIA savyá- ‘left-hand’ (13292 with Pk. savva- ‘left-hand’ and M. sav ‘the north’) which reflects PIE *(H)seȗȋo- ‘left (hand)’ (Mayrhofer) resp. *seyós ‘left’ (Mallory and Adams). The PIE source of OIA áva- ‘off, away, down’ is PIE *h4eu ‘away (from)’ and, according to Pokorny (IEW: 73), the Germanic cognate of OIA avás is found in Old High German westar ‘westward’, Old Norse vestr ‘west’, etc. < PIE *ȗes-t(e)ro-. Vamam Shivaram Apte shows in his dictionary (contrary to Monier-Williams, except ávara- i.a. ‘western’) that a semantic element ‘west’ is also found in other Sanskrit words: avanata- ‘verging in the west’, avanati- ‘declining in the west’. Regarding the obvious semantic relation between ‘west’ and ‘evening’ cf. also a possible paral- lel in Pog. varnɨ ‘evening’ and its likely association with OIA vāruṇī ‘the west’ (p. 233). Note: there is also Pr. vaċerˈa, vaċig, vaċˈeš ‘evening’. The first allomorph vaċerˈa resembles strikingly OCS večerǔ ‘evening’ which derives < PIE *wékeros ‘evening’. This can hardly be the same derivation for the Prasun lemma which rather may derive < OIA lex. utsūra- ‘the time when the sun sets, the evening’.

rows.etymology: 1230. Ku. bharsīt ‘midnight’ (with -sīt ← sitaṇ ‘to fall asleep’ < OIA supti- ‘sleep’ [13480] with epenthesis), MKH (1: 308) bharīe dharɔtīe ‘at midnight’ and Kiũṭh. dharātī ‘at midnight’ (H. ādhīrāt) — Bur. góne babár ‘midnight’ (with  gon ‘dawn’ and “bubber” ‘equal, level’ [Biddulph]), Kal. dubárabar rat ‘midnight’, Wg. dübarabˈar vātr ‘midnight’, Kt. rōtar brābar ‘midnight’, Kho. čhˈuybarabˈar ‘midnight’ with first component < OIA kṣapá- ‘night’ (3652) — Yid. barābar xšovo ‘midnight’ — probably also Ahīrī dialect of Bhil. ābārī rāt “much night” (LSI [ix, iii: 81]). There are Bur. babár ‘a half’ and Kal. barabár ‘half’ (← Pers. barābar?), the basic meaning of the forms thus corresponds to OIA ardharātra- ‘midnight’ which is e.g. found in Jaṭ. adh rāt ‘midnight’, Ku. poet. adhoratə, Kṭg. and Kc. adhe rāc ‘midnight’, Sōṇḍwāṛī dialect of Rj.mal. adhᵃrāt ‘midnight’, in Tor. “urẓāt” ‘mid-night’ (Biddulph), in B.chit. and B.roh. ada-rait (with epenthesis), and as borrowing in Kh. adharait ‘midnight’. But there are also Kt. samorut ‘mid-night’ (Biddulph) (with first element < OIA sāmí- ‘half’ which is otherwise without modern reflexes) and mílřādor ‘midnight’ which is < OIA madhyarātri- ‘midnight’ and which has a parallel in Ko.kuṇ. məndarrat ‘midnight’.

rows.etymology: 42. Bng. khəmbarɔ n.m. ‘body of a living or human being’ (used by shamans and therefore not easily verifiable) — Cf. Kal. khamíl or khamín ‘body, being’ (here perhaps also kạmbạhúki ‘doll; flag made in someone’s honor when he dies’ and kạmbạútyak ‘doll; festival of dolls’) — Korku kombor, komor ‘(physical) body’, Sant. hɔɽmɔ ‘the body – fig. tribe, sept’, Mu. hɔɽmɔ, Ho homo, Bir. hoɽmo all ‘(physical) body’. See Pinnow (K455) who refers to Bodding’s suggestion of connecting the lemma with Sant. hɔɽ ‘man, person, etc.’ (and thus also e.g. with Kh. kɑɽ, kʌɽ, kɔɽ ‘man, person, etc.’) but which cannot be the origin of the forms with -m-. Therefore, cf. Ju. kambulɔg, kamulɔg ‘man’ (with last syllable apparently also meaning ‘man’ – see SEAlang) and perhaps Tampuan kama̤k ‘man, male’.

rows.etymology: 312. Bng. kãṇḍi laṇɔ v.i. (n.f.) ‘to recite prayers, mantras’ < OIA kaṇṭhá- ‘voice’ (2680.c) with modern reflexes in Kt., Pr., Paš., and Gaw., to which are to be added Pal. khóṇḍa ‘to speak, talk, discuss, say’, Kal. khuṇḍiˈ-ek ‘to call out’ (Parkes 1991: 100), khóṇḍi mon ‘message or spoken word’, khuṇḍiék ‘to call, summon, speak’ and unaspirated kóṇḍik ‘to teach by using many examples’ (Trail and Cooper), and New. kāṇḍ ‘canto’. The OIA lemma 2680 is certainly the product of contamination of several originally separate lemmata and would have probably better been broken down into more lemmata. In any case, here also belong Bng. (2680a) (Pa., Pk.) kɔ̃ṭh ‘neck, throat’ and kãṭhɔ ‘collar; shoulder of a jacket’, (2680.b) kã̀ḍɔ1 n.m. ‘forest, hill, the (middle) area of human habitation (between valley ground and high peaks)’ (with parallels in West Pahāṛī “kanda” ‘high pasturing slopes and meadows’ [Handa 1998: 73], Kal. khaṇḍér ‘mountain pass’, Bal. kaṇḍ ‘hill pass’ and in P. kaṇḍhī ‘land bordering on a mountain’) and kãḍɔ2 n.m. ‘side (of a place)’; Bng. poet. khɔ̃ḍɔ ‘corner; end’, and Bng. (2680.d) (Pk.) kɔ̃ḍ(u)arɔ ‘side in a room where the door is’ (with -arɔ suffix?).

rows.gloss: person who speaks through his nose (as because of a cleft palate)
rows.etymology: 62. Garh. guganyāṭu ‘one who speaks through the nose’ and guganyāṇu ‘to speak in nasal sound, speak through the nose’, probably Bng. poet. gũ̀giaṇɔ ‘to cause (a pig) to grunt’, P. guṅguṇāuṇā ‘to speak through the nose’ and guṇguṇ ‘speaking through the nose, mumbling’ — Kal. gruṅgústi ‘person who speaks through his nose (as because of a cleft palate)’ (-gústi probably a vālā suffix) — OIA (Galanos’ dictionary) guṃ-kvaṇa- ‘speaking through the nose’ — Sant. ghaŋ ghuŋ ‘through the nose, with a twang’ and g(h)ene g(h)ene ‘with a nasal twang, through the nose’, Bon. kuŋkaŋ ‘one who speaks in a nasal tone’ — Khmer kŋuə ‘to be nasal (of the voice)’. An ex. from the PAN describing Bhīmsen’s execution of a sacrifice in Kurukṣetra: paṭhi kaṭi-eri, sũgūr gũgiaɔ, kukṛi phɔtphɔtai kid cut-see.PP.F, pig make-grunt.PP.M.SG, chicken make-flutter.PP.F ‘a kid was cut, a pig was made to grunt, a chicken was made to flutter’[901]635 Note: Regarding Bng. phɔtphɔtaṇɔ ‘to make flutter’ cf. Garh. phaphtāṭ ‘sound of fluttering of a bird’ and Greek potáomai ‘flutter’, and PN *pʰatʰ- ‘to flutter’ (110). For related ‘butterfly’ words see p. 825.

rows.etymology: 1. Kho. kakhˈači n. ‘stuttering’, Kal. kakháči ‘unable to speak well; stutterer’ — cf. Temiar kag ‘to stutter, to stammer’, Proto-South Bahnaric *gaʔ ‘stammer’ and Sre gaʔ ‘stammer’, Phong kɯːk ‘stammer, stutter’, Palaung gɯʔ, gɯk ‘to stammer, stutter’. But there are also similar forms in Tibeto-Burman: Western Himalayish Bunan khì kare ‘stutter, stammer’, Tibetan and Sherpa kha khle ‘stutter, stammer’, Newar khakhɔ ‘stutter, stammer’.

origin_lemma.gloss: lump, clod, piece; mouthful, ball of rice &c.; calf of leg
origin_lemma.etymology: 8168 píṇḍa m. 'lump, clod, piece' RV., 'mouthful, ball of rice &c.' Gr̥Śr., 'calf of leg' Mālatīm., piṇḍaka- m.n. 'lump' Suśr., °ḍī- f. 'lump, lump of food' Āpast., °ḍikā- f. 'any fleshy swelling, esp. calf of leg' Yājñ. (cf. piṇḍilá- 'having large calves' lex. and → Psht. paṇḍaī 'calf of leg' EVP 57). [For 'lump' see also piḍaka-, *pēṇḍa-, *pēṇḍha-, *pēḍa-, *pēḍha-, *pēnda-, *pēntha, *puṇḍa-, *pōdda-, *pōnda-. This variety of phonetic form suggests non-Aryan (← Mu. PMWS 142, 162; ← Drav. T. Burrow TPS 1946, 23) rather than IE. origin EWA ii 275. P. Thieme's derivation < *piṁṣṭa- (ZDMG 93, 133) is phonetically unacceptable]
origin_lemma.tags: m RV Gr̥Śr Mālatīm Early-Vedic Classical

rows.gloss: round or cylindrical stone for breaking or kneading things like walnuts or salt
rows.etymology: 145. Kal. iṣṭíḷak ‘round or cylindrical stone for breaking or kneading things like walnuts or salt’ < OIA *viṣṭyā- ‘stiffen’ ← STYĀ ‘firm up, stiffen, coagulate’ which is found in OIA viṣṭīmín- ‘having an erect penis’. Note that PIE *sth2ei- ‘become hard, fixed’ is generally seen as the origin of ‘stone’ (German Stein).

rows.etymology: 221. Kal. uṣṭú ‘rock salt’ is possibly cognate with OIA aṣṭhi- ‘seed; a kernel, a stone’; cf. also aṣṭhīlā- ‘a globular body; a round pebble or stone; kernel; seed-corn’; it is possible that these OIA words are cognate with OIA áśman- ‘stone’ (see EWA sub aṣṭhīvánt- ‘the knee, knee-bone’).

rows.gloss: to burn or smart (as salt in a wound)
rows.etymology: 519. (a) Bng. cəś ‘burning pain’, Kc. ċaśiṇo ‘to be burnt (e.g. hand on hot iron)’, Deog. and Jaun. ciśṇɔ ‘to burn one’s hand etc.’, Him. cośṇu ‘to burn with fire’, P. cīs ‘a sharp pain’, Ku. ciśṇō ‘to burn’, ciśi ‘scare of fire’ and cis ‘keen pain, scorching’, cisuk ‘very cold’, N. ciso ‘wet, cold’, Kgr. cas ‘slipped disc’ — Ind. c̣ʌ̀ṣ ‘sudden fierce or stabbing pain; lumbago; a touch’ and c̣ʌ̀s ‘sudden fierce or stabbing pain’, Kal. čičiék ‘to burn or smart (as salt in a wound)’. The words are to be seen in connection (i) with OIA *cassakk- ‘throb, twitch, sudden pain’ (4730), *cīssa- ‘sharp pain’ (4847), caṣati² ‘hurts’ (4727a), chaṣati ‘hurts’ (Dhātup.) (the aspirated form is reflected in Garh. chasāk ‘nukīlī vastu kī halkī cubhan - slight sting or piercing through a pointed object’), cahakk- ‘burn brightly’ (4731) (with debuccalisation), and perhaps cāṣa-  ‘sugarcane’ (4774) (see there G. cās ‘boiled syrup’), and (ii) with OIA *atyuṣati ‘burns’, *atyoṣati, *atyuṣyate ‘is burnt’ (226a), and (iii) perhaps with Dravidian DEDR kiccu (1514): Tam. kiccu ‘fire’, Tel. ciccu ‘fire, flame’ etc. which is perhaps worth comparing with Garh.nā. cac-kār, cac-gār ‘very cold’ (with -kār suffix). The Bng. and Deog. forms go back to older *c̣aṣ-, but not the Kc. form which therefore must be an early borrowing at a time when Proto-Bangāṇī and Proto-Deogārī still had three sibilants but Proto-Kocī only two. See next and next but one. (b) Like in the preceding paragraph, also in this paragraph semantic-morphological amalgamations (see p. 224) have been rampant. Bng. jàṣṇɔ ‘to singe s.o. (e.g., with an iron rod)’, invol. jàśiṇɔ, jìśaiṇɔ ‘to singe o.s. badly’ (with -ai- suffix), Garh. jhās ‘slight neuralgia or birth pangs’, jhasāk ‘touch through fire or nettle’ and jhusmus ‘dawn, early morning’ — here also A. zah ‘heat, summer’? — Pal. jhāṣˈī ‘caterpillar’ (contact with some types causes severe allergic reactions), Tor. j̣eṣ ([jyɛṣ]) ‘caterpillar’, K. zᵃj ‘a certain tiny longish insect, similar to an ant, which by coṅtact with the skin causes irritation and scratching’, Dari. jhusili kirā ‘caterpillar’ and Garh. jhissu or jhijju ‘ek roẽdār kīṛā – a hairy worm’ and jhusalyā ‘person with unwanted hair on his face or body’ and Kho. ǰaláṣ ‘hairy (person); a disheveled, long-haired person’ derive either/or or both < OIA lex. jhaṣa- ‘sun-heat’ (5359) or < OIA *adhyuṣyate ‘is lighted up, burnt’ (280a) with a modern reflex in Kṭg. There is also Bng. ujà̄śɔ n.m. ‘the power that induces spontaneous possession (e.g., during the approaching of a deity towards a village); splendour of the sun’ (with retention of palatal feature because of coronal consonant harmony) which is < related OIA *ujjhāṣa- ‘shining’ (1678) (Pk.) with one modern parallel in G. to which is to be added Br.-Aw. ujās ‘light; gleam’, and Bng. jà̄ś n.f. ‘tension, stress, impulse, cheering up’ which also derives < OIA lex. *jhaṣa- ‘sun-heat’ (5359). (c) Bng. kiśaiṇɔ or ciśaiṇɔ ‘to scorch children in jest with glowing charcoal’ (the lat- ter form is apparently cognate with forms listed in paragraph [a]), Khaś. kreśśnū ͡ and Bhad. ṭlessnū ‘cries due to physical pain’ (Kaul [2006 i: 305]) < OIA *kreśayati ‘presses’ (3606) (but regarding semantics compare cognate OIA kleśayati ‘torments’) with a modern parallel in Dm., but the verb has further parallels in Roh. (3588), Kal. (3589), K. (3590, 3591) and Wg. (3605). Notes: (a) Despite the massive semantic-morphological amalgamations one wonders whether above alternation of Bng. kiśaiṇɔ ∼ ciśaiṇɔ ‘to scorch . . . with glow- ing charcoal’ does not indicate a reflex of OIA KĀŚ ‘shine, look brilliant’ which may be also reflected in Bng. cɔṣṇɔ ‘to light, ignite, burn s.th. or s.o.’, cɔśkɔ i.a. ‘a sudden and short apparition (e.g. of a ghost or of a god in a medium)’ and perhaps in cɔkśɔ, cɔkśelɔ ‘shining, radiant’ if this is reflex of older *caśaka-(illa-) (extended with -kɔ2 suffix [and MIA -illa- suffix). In such a case it could be morphologically compared with OIA cáṣṭe ‘appears’. This interpretations seems semantically more plausible than borrowing from Dravidian. (b) The same OIA root in form of cākṣuṣá- ‘relating to sight’ is perhaps the origin of Kal. čákaš ‘cowrie shell’ which, regarding basic meaning, cf. with Kal. čákaš čhína ‘animal with white mark on its face’ (with second word < OIA cihna- ‘mark, sign’ [4833] and aspiration fronting).
